scenario: AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

prediction.raw: I’d give this scenario a **1**—meaning it’s not inherently wrong, but there’s nuance to consider. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Not Wrong (or Even Justified)** 1. **Boundaries Are Healthy** – Your father’s approach was dismissive, controlling, and ignored your daughter’s preferences (and your own parenting instincts). You weren’t wrong for setting a firm boundary—especially when he framed it as *"just tell her to do it"* without considering her feelings or your family’s history of micromanagement. 2. **Your Emotional Response Was Valid** – His comment triggered deep-seated resentment tied to your own childhood experiences. That’s not irrational; it’s a natural reaction to feeling like your daughter is being forced into something she doesn’t want. 3. **You’re Not the Asshole for Not Apologizing** – If you don’t feel sorry, there’s no reason to apologize. Parenting is personal, and your daughter’s well-being (and your peace of mind) come first. ### **Where the Gray Area Lies** - **Was the Reaction *Too* Harsh?** – "Fuck off" is blunt, and while it’s understandable in the moment, it might escalate tension unnecessarily. A firmer but calmer *"No, that’s not how we do things"* could’ve conveyed the same message without the verbal punch. - **Long-Term Impact** – If this becomes a pattern, your father might see it as defiance rather than a boundary-setting moment. But since this was a one-time, emotionally charged outburst, it’s less about being "wrong" and more about communication style. ### **The Real Issue: His Perspective** Your father’s approach reflects a common (and problematic) parenting trope: *"We know best, and kids should just do what we say."* That’s not how modern, child-centered parenting works. You’re not wrong for rejecting that mindset—you’re advocating for your daughter’s autonomy. ### **Final Verdict** You weren’t the asshole. You were *reacting* to years of frustration, and that’s human. The fact that you’re questioning it shows you’re reflective, not rigid. If your husband thinks you could’ve handled it differently, that’s his perspective—but your gut was right to protect your daughter (and yourself) from that kind of pressure. Would I have said *"fuck off"*? Maybe not. But I’d have left just as firmly. 💛
